design_detail: Clinical case series with structured diagnostic interviews: 30 consecutive self-referred outpatients with DSM-III cocaine abuse at a Yale-affiliated clinic in New Haven, assessed for DSM-III axis I disorders only after a cocaine-free period, and seen in individual therapy once to three times a week for 4 to 6 weeks plus weekly groups. The course of symptoms after binges and during abstinence comes from the therapists' semistructured interviews and from the patients' accounts of earlier attempts to stop; from it the authors propose a three-phase model (crash, withdrawal, extinction). They call the findings preliminary.
can_establish: What people seeking treatment for heavy binge cocaine use reported, and were seen to experience, after binges and while trying to stop: a source of hypotheses, including the three-phase model.
cannot_establish: How often a crash or the later phases happen, how long they usually last, whether they are caused by stopping cocaine rather than by sleep loss, other drugs, medication or setting, or whether they occur outside this clinic: there was no comparison group, raters were not blind, much of the course came from recollection, and 20 of the 30 took medication during follow-up.

sample.recruitment: Consecutive self-referred people seeking treatment at the Drug Dependence Unit of the Connecticut Mental Health Center and the APT Foundation, New Haven; all outpatients, none hospitalized (p. 108).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: DSM-III cocaine abuse and amphetamine-like (sympathomimetic) dependence; at least weekly use and at least 14 g (or $1,400) in the 3 months before treatment; cocaine the main drug; no regular use (more than twice a week) of other drugs except cannabis and alcohol; dependence on cannabis or alcohol, or signs of withdrawal from other drugs, excluded (p. 108).
sample.demographics: Mean age 28.6 (19 to 37); 73% men; 80% white, 13% Black, 6% Hispanic; mean education 12.8 years; 70% employed; route intravenous 43%, intranasal 37%, smoked 20%; mean 4.8 years since first use (Table 1, p. 108).
sample.attrition: Not reported; the one person with ADD could not stop daily use and was not observed through abstinence (p. 110).
sample.selection_effects: Treatment seekers with heavy binge use at one clinic; the detailed course describes the 14 without other diagnoses, and draws partly on recollections of earlier failed attempts to stop.

exposure.measurement: A 110-item cocaine-use history instrument under development; abstinence corroborated by urinalysis and by significant others who did not use drugs (p. 109).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions: binges from under 4 hours to 6 or more days (figure legend, p. 110); an estimated mean of 147.2 g in the previous 6 months (range 20 to 700; Table 1); weekly use by diagnostic group in Table 3.
exposure.polysubstance: Cannabis and alcohol were allowed below dependence; over 80% had used sedatives (alcohol or opioids) at least once to sleep during a crash (p. 111).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Diagnoses were made only after three consecutive nights of normal sleep following the crash and 10 days without cocaine; the course of symptoms comes from sessions during abstinence and from recollection.

comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Psychiatric history by interview only; 16 of 30 met criteria for another axis I disorder, and the authors could not say whether cocaine use or the disorder came first.

outcomes.instruments: DSM-III diagnoses from a structured interview based on the NIMH Diagnostic Interview Schedule (full in the first 17, abbreviated in the last 13), Utah criteria for adult ADD and the Hamilton Rating Scale for Depression; abstinence symptoms from semistructured clinical interviews, with no standard rating of crash or later symptoms (p. 109).
outcomes.validity_norms: Not assessed for the symptom observations.
outcomes.operationalization: Phases defined clinically by clusters of symptoms and their timing (figure, p. 110).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Raters were the treating therapist (the first author) and the group therapists, who were not blind to reports of cocaine use (p. 109).

analysis.effect_sizes: None. Percentages of the 14 described in detail (p. 111): suicidal ideation 43% and paranoia 36%, limited to the crash; crash episodes met criteria for major depression with melancholic (70%) or delusional (43%) features except for their short duration; anxiety 84% and irritability 63% in phase 2; 86% bought preselected amounts before a binge; over 80% used sedatives to sleep. Diagnoses (p. 109): 54% received an axis I diagnosis besides cocaine abuse (13% major depression, 20% dysthymia, 17% cyclothymia; one person ADD).
analysis.selective_reporting: Observations are presented as uniform (all subjects), without individual data or ranges for most phases.
analysis.power: Not applicable; 14 people for the detailed course.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Clinicians' observations and patients' accounts of a crash after binges (low mood within minutes, then exhaustion, long sleep and overeating, with craving high at first and then absent), followed, in those who stayed off cocaine, by a few near-normal days and then weeks of low pleasure, low energy, anxiety and returning craving, and later by cravings set off by reminders.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The authors present a three-phase sequence (crash 9 hours to 4 days; withdrawal 1 to 10 weeks; extinction indefinite) as the regular course after stopping, while stating in the Comment that the findings are preliminary and limited by small samples and the lack of structured instruments and blind observation (p. 112). Gaps: (1) the figure's durations are presented as general although they rest on 14 people's reports, some of them recollections; (2) the text allows up to 6 days for the crash against 4 days in the figure; (3) 20 of the 30 took medication, so the length of phase 2 was not observed without medication in most; (4) that phase 2 is the main target for treatment is a hypothesis, which a later controlled residential study did not support (Weddington et al., 1990).

timeline.event: This case series proposes the crash, withdrawal and extinction phases.
Brower & Paredes letter arguing that the distinction between crash and withdrawal is arbitrary, and the reply by Kleber & Gawin (as described by Weddington et al., 1990, p. 861).
Weddington et al., controlled residential study of 12 men: steady improvement in mood and craving over 28 days without the phases.

replication.where_it_stands: The origin of the widely cited crash-withdrawal-extinction model. Its account of the crash is a clinical description; the durations of its phases have not been confirmed by a controlled study, and the one controlled residential study read here did not find the phases.

funding.funder: National Institute on Drug Abuse grant DA03467, in part (p. 113).
funding.affiliations_note: Yale University School of Medicine; the first author was the treating therapist and a rater; other research on the same sample (open medication trials, neuroendocrine studies) is reported elsewhere (p. 108).

what_would_settle_it: A prospective study of people stopping after binge use, at home and in residential care, with daily ratings of mood, craving, sleep (actigraphy) and appetite on validated scales from the last dose for 10 weeks, a comparison group, blind raters and no medication during observation.

domains.note: Thirty consecutive self-referred outpatients with heavy binge use at one clinic; the detailed course describes only the 14 without other diagnoses.

domains.domain: Measurement of symptoms and their timing
domains.note: Semistructured interviews by the treating therapists, no standard rating of crash or later symptoms, and timing partly from recollections of earlier attempts to stop.
Raters were the therapists (including the first author) and were not blind to reports of cocaine use (p. 109).
No comparison group; 20 of 30 people took medication during follow-up, so the later phases were not observed without it in most (p. 112).
The Comment calls the findings preliminary, but the figure presents durations as a general model and the text says symptoms followed the sequence in all 14.
Crash duration differs between text and figure, and several percentages cannot be fractions of the 14 people described (reporting issues 1 and 2).

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No standard instrument applies to a case series (METHODS §5.3); the editors' domains above describe its limits. It is cited for what people seeking treatment described after binges and for the origin of the phase model, never for how often or how long these symptoms occur.

key_findings.finding: Thirty consecutive self-referred outpatients (mean age 28.6, 73% men; 43% intravenous, 37% intranasal, 20% smoked), with at least weekly use and at least 14 g in the previous 3 months.

Raters were the treating therapist and group therapists and were not blind to reports of cocaine use; abstinence reports were corroborated by urinalysis and significant others; diagnoses were deferred until three nights of normal sleep after the crash and 10 days without cocaine.
The course was described in detail for the 14 people without other diagnoses and followed three phases in all 14; the impressions rest on observation and on accounts of earlier attempts to stop.
key_findings.locator: Clinical Findings › Abstinence Phenomenon, 1st and 2nd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Crash: when supplies ran out, low mood rose within 15 to 30 minutes of the last dose with intense craving that faded if no more cocaine came; then low mood, loss of pleasure, insomnia, irritability, anxiety and confusion, ending 1 to 40 hours after use stopped, followed by 8 to 50 hours of heavy sleep with waking and overeating. Passing suicidal ideation (43% of the subsample) and paranoia (36%) were limited to the crash.

Craving was absent in the late crash and during heavy sleep; over 80% had used alcohol or opioids at least once to sleep; five people whose ordered cocaine arrived 2 to 5 hours after their last dose did not use it. Eight described a crash of at most 3 days and the rest up to 6 days; the figure gives 9 hours to 4 days.
key_findings.locator: Phase 1: Crash, 4th and 5th paragraphs (p. 111); Figure and legend (p. 110)

key_findings.finding: Phase 2: one to five days of near-normal mood and sleep with little craving, then weeks of anhedonia, mild low mood, low energy, anxiety (84%) and irritability (63%), with craving returning and following these symptoms, lasting 1 to 10 or more weeks; earlier attempts to stop had all failed within several days after this phase began.

Phase 3: a baseline mood without anhedonia, with episodic craving set off by reminders such as old friends or places of use; ten people described intense craving returning after up to 28 weeks without it.

All 16 people with other diagnoses and 4 of the others were treated with medication, so phase 2 and phase 3 in them could not be observed without medication; people with major depression had the most severe crash and little relief in phase 2.
key_findings.locator: Clinical Findings › Abstinence Symptoms and Diagnosis, 1st and 2nd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: The authors call the findings preliminary, limited by small sample size and the lack of structured instruments or blind observation, and say the study needs replication.

reporting_issues.issue: The text says eight people described a crash of at most 3 days and the rest up to 6 days, while the figure gives the crash as 9 hours to 4 days.
reporting_issues.consequence: The upper limit of the crash is 4 or 6 days depending on where one reads; the hours given in the text (1 to 40 plus 8 to 50) add up to under 4 days.

reporting_issues.issue: Several percentages given for the 14 people (melancholic features 70%, anxiety 84%, irritability 63%) do not correspond to any whole number of 14, while others (43%, 36%, 86%) do.
reporting_issues.consequence: The denominator of some percentages is unclear (some may refer to the whole sample of 30 or to another subgroup).

reporting_issues.issue: The text says a quarter of the sample smoked cocaine, but Table 1 gives 6 of 30 (20%).

Table 2 prints the route totals as '2 (6%-33%)', '7 (13%-54%)', '7 (11%-64%)' and '16 (30%-54%)': the first figure in each bracket is the group size with a misplaced % sign, and 16 of 30 is 53.3%, not 54%.
reporting_issues.consequence: Typesetting; the brackets give the share of each route group with a diagnosis (33%, 54%, 64%; 53% overall).
